title: WombatLM
subtitle: A tiny model learns animal word forms
form.name: same name
form.tip.name: Write the animal’s name unchanged (slon → slon). The model practises this to learn copying letters.
form.tip.male: Write the word for the male animal.
form.tip.female: Write the word for the female animal.
form.tip.young: Write the word for the young animal.
badge.hidden: 🔒 hidden real answer (never seen in training)
badge.invention: ✨ its own invention (no real word in the data)
confidenceHelp: How sure the model is of the whole word. A sure answer can still be wrong!
score.close: never seen, right or one letter off
att.title: Where it looks
att.help: Each row is one letter of the answer. Dark cells show which letters of the animal the model looked at while writing it (each row adds up to 100). ✱ is the task (which language and form). Point at a row or at a guess column to link them.
att.decSelf: Looking back at its own answer (head {n})
att.encSelf: Animal letters looking at each other (head {n})
map.title: Letter map
map.help: Letters that play the same part in words end up close together. Find the vowels (red circles): at the start they are scattered, and after a few thousand steps they gather into one group.
map.how: How the map is made: the model keeps a list of 32 numbers for every letter (its letter table) and learns them. 32 numbers cannot be drawn, so the map squeezes them flat onto the two directions where the letters differ the most. Letters the model treats alike get similar numbers, so they land close together.
map.note: The flat map keeps only about {p} % of the differences between the letters, so two letters can look close without being alike. The list of closest letters uses all 32 numbers.
map.pick: Click a letter to see the letters the model treats most alike.
map.rare: {letter} appears only {n}× in the learning data, so the model has learned little about it. Its closest letters are mostly chance.
inside.intro: This model has {n} numbers. ChatGPT-class models have hundreds of billions.
inside.help: Every square is one number of the model. Learning means nudging these numbers a tiny bit after every batch of examples. The weights themselves look like noise; the change shows where it is learning right now.
inside.note.delta: how much each number changed in the last {n} steps
inside.note.grad: which way each number wants to move after the batch of step {step}
inside.note.gradNone: no gradient yet: train at least one step
inside.groupHelp.letters: One row of numbers per letter and per position. The same letter table is used for reading the animal and for choosing the next letter.
inside.groupHelp.encoder: The letters of the animal look at each other and think, so each letter knows its neighbours.
inside.groupHelp.decoder: Letter by letter: look back at the answer so far, look at the animal, think, then guess the next letter.
signal.title: Follow the signal
signal.help: The numbers each position carries on its way through the model, for {word}. One row per letter, one column per number.
inside.note.delta1: how much each number changed in the last step
build.title: Learning
build.help: Learning happens only here: while ▶ Play runs, or when you press Step. In every step the model practises a few examples whose answers it knows, measures its mistakes and nudges all its numbers a little. Nothing else changes the model.
practice.title: What it's practising now
practice.help: This is the learning data of the latest step ({shown} of {batch} examples): questions together with their right answers. Before learning from them, the model answers them the ordinary way. Then it compares its answers with the right ones (that is the mistake, or loss) and nudges all its numbers a little so that next time the right answers come out more likely.
practice.empty: Nothing yet. Press ▶ Play or Step ×1 to start learning.
cycle.title: One learning step
cycle.hint: Tip: pause, then press Step ×1 to watch one step slowly.
cycle.running: This repeats about {n} times a second.
ask.title: Answering
ask.help: Pick a language, type an animal and choose which word you want, then press a button. Answering sends your word through the model once, letter by letter. The model's numbers are only read, never changed: the same model always gives the same answer. While it is learning, the answer waits until it pauses or you press “Ask again”.
stamp.fresh: 🔒 Answer from the model at step {step}. Answering never changes the model.
stamp.stale: ⏳ The model has learned {n} more steps since this answer (step {step}).
practice.explain: Learning data = questions with their right answers. The model answers them first, then compares with the right answers and nudges its numbers.
practice.noAnswers: It was learning too fast to answer each batch. Press Step ×1 to see it answer them.
data.title: What it learns from
data.explain: All of the data, as questions and their right answers. The model learns from most of the animals: each training step picks a few learning examples at random (see the Model learning tab). The never-seen animals are only used for testing: they show whether it has learned the pattern or only memorised the words.
data.help: In the overview table every yellow word is one learning example: "animal name → this form". The name column is the copy practice: "write the name unchanged" (it helps the model learn to copy letters). A dash means the language has no real word for that form, so there is nothing to learn there; the model can still invent one if you ask. Click any word (or any question in "Every question") to see it as tokens, the way the model learns it.
data.col.name: Name (copy it)
data.tip.learned: Learning example: {from} → {to}. Click to see it as tokens.
data.tip.copy: Learning example: copy the name, {word} → {word}. Click to see it as tokens.
data.tip.missing: No real word in this language: not in the learning data.
data.tip.kept: Never-seen animal: the model does not learn from it, it is only tested on it. Click to see it as tokens.
data.tip.hidden: Hidden: tick "show the never-seen answers" to see it.
data.given.title: What the model is given:
data.given.body: for each question only a task token (language + form, e.g. "Czech, female") and the letters of the animal's name; when learning, also the right answer, letter by letter. Never the animal's id, its pack, its name in the other language, or whether it is never seen: those only decide which questions it learns from and which it is tested on.
data.view.table.tip: One row per animal: the name and its male / female / young words.
data.view.questions.tip: Every question exactly as the model gets it, its answers, and what it is used for.
data.view.records.tip: The data itself, every field, as stored in the data files.
data.view.table.note: A short overview: one row per animal in one language.
data.view.questions.note: Every question, one per line, exactly as the model gets it: the task token and the name. Next to it: the right answer, and whether the question is used for learning, for testing, or both.
data.view.records.note: The data records as stored in the data files (all languages together), with every field. Only names and forms ever reach the model; the other fields decide how they are used.
data.q.shown: {n} questions shown: {learn} learned from, {test} tested with a right answer, {invent} tested with no real word (it invents), {unused} not used (names of never-seen animals).
data.q.col.question: Question (what the model reads)
data.rec.id: the animal's id in the data file. Never given to the model.
data.rec.pack: which data file (pack) it comes from. Never given to the model.
data.rec.names: the animal's name in each language. Given to the model: it is what it reads, and "copy the name" is learned from it.
data.rec.forms: male / female / young word in each language. The right answers it learns, or (never-seen animals) is tested on. A missing form means there is no real word.
data.rec.unseen: marks a never-seen animal ("unseen": true): only tested, never learned. Without it the model learns from the animal. Never given to the model.
test.title: Test: what it answers for every animal
test.explain: An automatic check, not needed to understand the model. The model is asked every form of every animal, and each answer is compared with the learning data. Nothing is learned from it: the model stays exactly the same. Never-seen animals are tested too: they show whether it learned the pattern or only memorised the words. It is tested only while this tab is open (every 100 training steps), so learning is not slowed down otherwise.
test.help: This is an exam, not learning data: the words in the table are the model's own answers. ✓ right, ≈ one letter off, ✗ wrong. ✨ means the language has no real word for that form, so whatever it wrote is its own invention (those are re-tested every 500 steps). Hover over a word to see the right one; click it to ask the question on the Ask the model tab.
test.scoreHelp: How many it answers right, at each test so far (it is tested only while this tab is open).
askStatus.learning: The model is at step {step} and learning right now.
askStatus.paused: The model is at step {step}, paused.
tok.form.name: name
tok.tip.unk: Unknown letter: the model has no token for it, so it reads “?” instead.
tok.tip.task: Task token: tells the model what to write ({name}).
tok.tip.end: End of the word: writing this token means “I am done”.
tokens.title: Tokens: what goes in and what comes out
tokens.help: The model cannot read letters. Every word is cut into tokens, and every token is a number: its place in the list of all tokens the model knows. Here one token is one letter. The question starts with a task token that says what to write (which language and form). The answer comes out one token at a time; the model stops by writing the “end” token. Point at a token of the answer to see its guesses below.
tokens.note: The model never sees letters, only these numbers. Here one token is one letter: it knows {n} different tokens. Big chat models cut text into pieces of words instead, with about 100,000 different tokens.
tokens.unk: The model has no token for {chars}: it reads “?” instead and cannot tell what it was.
example.title: One learning example, as tokens
example.pick: Click a word in the table to see how the model learns it.
example.question: {lang}, {form}: {from} → {to}
example.shown: It is shown the answer so far
example.guess: It must guess the next token
example.explain: This one example is {n} guesses. Before each guess the model is shown the right answer so far (the row above) and must guess the next token (the row below): the same answer, shifted by one. The loss is how wrong these {n} guesses are, on average. All of them are checked at once, in one training step.
example.kept: Never-seen animal: the model never learns from it, it is only tested on it, so there are no guesses to learn here.
quiet.label: Quiet learning (faster)
quiet.help: While it learns, skip the pictures: no testing, no answering the batch first, no letter map or weights. Everything updates again when you pause.
quiet.note: Quiet learning is on: the pictures wait until you pause.
goal.label: Learn until
goal.help: Learning stops by itself at this step. Around step 2,500 the model knows most animals it learns from, around 5,000 almost all of them. After that its answers barely change, so more steps mostly mean waiting. You can still press Step, or pick a higher goal to keep learning.
goal.reached: Done: it learned until step {n}. Pick a higher goal to keep learning.
practice.letterTip: {char}: it gave the right letter {p} % → mistake {m}
practice.lossTip: The average mistake over the letters of this answer (point at a letter to see its own).
practice.lossExplain: How the mistake is measured: the model is shown the right answer letter by letter and has to guess each next letter. A letter's mistake is how surprised it was by the right one: if it gave the right letter 100 %, the mistake is 0; 50 % → 0.69; 10 % → 2.3; 1 % → 4.6 (that is −ln of the chance). Redder letters surprised it more. A line's mistake is the average over its letters, and the step's mistake {loss} is the average over all {n} letters of all {b} examples. Learning nudges the numbers so that these mistakes get smaller. A right answer can still have a mistake: it was right, but not sure.
data.sum.learn.label: Learning
data.sum.learn: {examples} learning examples: {forms} word forms (male / female / young) + {copies} copy the name, from {train} animals
data.sum.test.label: Testing
data.sum.test: {tests} questions with a right answer, {unseenTests} of them from the {unseen} never-seen animals; {inventions} questions with no real word (it can only invent)
inside.guide: Start at the top: where the model is learning right now, then follow one letter of its answer through the model, number by number. The pictures of all its numbers are further down.
inside.shared: same colour scale for all pictures
inside.sharedHelp: On: a strong colour means a big number in every picture, so pictures can be compared. Off: each picture uses its own scale, which shows the pattern inside a picture better.
inside.val.delta: changed by {v} in the last steps
inside.val.grad: gradient: {v} (learning moves the number the opposite way)
tip.embed: Each letter is stored as {d} numbers; this is number {c} of {tok}. Letters used in a similar way end up with similar numbers.
tip.pos: Added to number {c} of whatever letter stands at position {r}, so the model knows where in the word it is.
tip.outBias: A head start for {tok} when guessing the next letter: higher means it is guessed more easily.
tip.Wq: How much number {r} of a letter adds to number {c} of its question (what it looks for).
tip.Wk: How much number {r} of a letter adds to number {c} of its label (what it offers to the others).
tip.Wv: How much number {r} of a letter adds to number {c} of what it passes on when someone looks at it.
tip.Wo: How much number {r} of what was collected adds to number {c} of the letter.
tip.ffnUp: How strongly number {r} of the letter switches on thinking unit {c}.
tip.ffnDown: How much thinking unit {r}, when it is on, adds to number {c} of the letter.
tip.ln.gamma: Volume knob of number {c}: 1 = unchanged, 0 = muted.
tip.ln.beta: Shift added to number {c} after the volume knob.
tip.bias: Starting value of {what}, added whatever comes in.
flow.title: Where is it learning?
flow.help: The model's parts in the order a word goes through them. The bar shows how much of each part's numbers changed per learning step lately (the same scale for every part); the line shows it over time while this tab is open. Click a part to see its numbers.
flow.end: guess the next letter (using the letter table again)
flow.dec.self: look back at the answer so far
explain.title: Look inside one letter
explain.help: Pick a letter of the answer. You see every number the model computes on the way to writing it: the letter going in, what each step adds (the biggest changes are outlined), and the final guess. Click any square or guess to see exactly where its value comes from.
explain.numbers: write the numbers in the squares
explain.noAnswer: Ask the model a question first (on the Ask the model tab).
explain.caption0: Writing letter 1 of {n}: nothing is written yet, the model only knows the task. It writes “{chosen}”.
explain.caption: Writing letter {k} of {n}: “{written}” is written so far. Now it writes “{chosen}”.
explain.marks: The numbers of the model this letter uses are outlined in orange in the pictures below.
explain.start.title: The last written letter goes in: {tok}
explain.start.help: Its row of the letter table plus the row for position {n}: {d} numbers. Every step below adds something to these numbers.
explain.self.title: Look back at the answer so far
explain.self.help: It compares what it looks for with what every earlier position offers, and mixes in what the best matches pass on. Each head looks on its own.
explain.cross.title: Look at the animal
explain.cross.help: The same, but it looks at the letters of the animal (after the model read them).
explain.ffn.title: Think
explain.ffn.help: The numbers switch thinking units on (red) or leave them off. Every unit that is on adds its own pattern of numbers.
explain.guess.title: Guess the next letter
explain.guess.help: After the last volume knobs, every letter gets a score: these numbers times its row of the letter table, plus its favourite-letter bonus. The scores become percentages (softmax).
explain.head: head {n}
explain.changeHelp: Size of what this step adds, compared with the size of the numbers before it
explain.click: click: where does it come from?
explain.d.start: Number {n}: {tok} from the letter table + {pos} for the position = {sum}.
explain.d.final: Number {n} after the volume knobs: {v}. Click a guess to see how it is used.
explain.d.score: Score of '{tok}' = {s} ({p} %). It is the sum of these numbers times its row of the letter table, plus its bonus:
explain.d.unitOn: Thinking unit {n} is on ({v}). When on, it adds its own pattern of numbers (its row in “thinking, part 2”).
explain.d.unitOff: Thinking unit {n} is (almost) off ({v}), so it adds (almost) nothing.
explain.d.addAttend: This step adds {v} to number {n}. Where it comes from:
explain.d.addThink: Thinking adds {v} to number {n}. Where it comes from:
ask.lookInside: Click a letter's column to look inside the model while it writes that letter.
ask.nowTip: Show the whole answer at once.
ask.slowTip: Watch the model write the answer one letter at a time: what it reads, which letters it weighs up, and which one it picks.
ask.prompt: Press “Answer now” to see the whole answer, or “Answer slowly” to watch the model write it letter by letter.
ask.word.known: ✓ an animal from the learning data ({lang})
ask.word.other: This word is in the {lang} learning data.
ask.word.free: Not an animal from the learning data: the model will have to make up an answer.
att.prompt: Ask the model something to see where it looks.
slow.readingDetail: It turns the task and each letter into numbers ({n} tokens) and looks at all of them together.
slow.picks: Its best guesses: {guesses} → it writes {chosen}. Each new letter looks back at the animal (attention, on the right).
slow.doneDetail: {n} guesses, one after another. Point at a column of the guesses to look at any letter again.
practice.checkTip: The same example measured again right after the nudge (the ordinary way, as when answering).
practice.checkExplain: After the step: the model was asked the same {b} examples again, before and after the nudge, measured the ordinary way (as when answering). Mistake before {before} → after {after}. The right letter became more likely in {up} letters and less likely in {down}. One small step does not fix everything: it moves every number only a tiny bit, in the direction that helps this batch as a whole. (The mistake used for learning, {step}, is a little different: while learning, 1 in 10 numbers is switched off at random, see “What this step changed”.)
practice.checkLetterTip: {char}: the right letter had {before} % before the step → {after} % after
practice.checkLossTip: Mistake of this example just before → just after the step
practice.checkAnswerTip: What it answers for this question now, after the step
inside.whyClick: Click: why did this number change in the last step?
signal.memory: after reading, with volume knobs (what the writer looks at)
signal.dec.final: after writing, with volume knobs (makes the guess)
sd.title: What this step changed
sd.help: One learning step, exactly: 1. the batch goes through the model and every letter's mistake is measured; 2. backpropagation sends the mistake back through the model, so every number gets its gradient: how much the mistake would grow if this number grew a little; 3. if all gradients together are too big, they are all shrunk by the same factor; 4. every number is nudged against its gradient by the Adam rule, which also remembers earlier steps; 5. the same examples are measured again. This is recorded only for Step ×1, because it costs as much as about 20 ordinary steps.
sd.empty: Pause and press Step ×1. The model then records that one learning step in full: the examples before and after, which numbers moved, and for any number the exact calculation of why it moved.
sd.running: Not shown while it learns continuously (recording one step costs as much as about 20 ordinary ones). Pause and press Step ×1.
sd.f.measureVal: mistake {loss}, with 1 in 10 numbers switched off at random (dropout)
sd.f.nudgeWarm: learning rate {lr}: warming up, step {t} of {w} (full rate {full})
sd.checkBetter: It helped: on the same {b} examples the mistake went from {before} to {after}. The right letter became more likely in {up} letters, less likely in {down}.
sd.checkWorse: This step did not help on its own batch: mistake {before} → {after}. The right letter became more likely in {up} letters, less likely in {down}. That happens: Adam remembers earlier steps, so a step also follows where earlier batches pushed.
sd.checkNote: Measured the ordinary way (nothing switched off), as when answering.
sd.moved: {moved} of its {total} numbers moved. The biggest move was {max}; half of the numbers moved by more than {median}. Every number moves a little, even ones this batch hardly touched: Adam keeps moving them in the direction of earlier steps.
sd.list.changeTip: The numbers whose value changed the most in this step
sd.list.pushTip: The numbers this batch wanted to change the most
sd.list.changeHelp: Numbers that moved the most in this step. With Adam, these are often numbers that rarely get a gradient: their step is not made smaller by a history of big gradients.
sd.list.pushHelp: Numbers with the biggest gradient: changing them would change this batch's mistake the most. They do not have to move the most: Adam divides each step by how big that number's gradients usually are.
sd.pickHint: Click a row to see why that number changed. You can also click any square in the pictures on the Inside the model tab.
sd.why.missing: This is no longer the latest step. Pause and press Step ×1 again.
sd.why.title: Why did it change? {name}
sd.why.summary: Before the step {before}, after {after} (change {d}). Here is the whole calculation.
sd.why.pushTitle: The gradient: which way would help?
sd.why.push: Gradient {g}: if this number grew by 0.01, the batch mistake would grow by about {small}. So learning moves it {way}.
sd.why.noSplit: The batch is too big to split into examples (more than 32).
sd.why.sharesHelp: The batch mistake is the average over all letters of all examples, so the gradient is exactly the sum of what each example contributes. An example contributes nothing if this number does not affect its letters.
sd.why.limitTitle: Limit: are all gradients together too big?
sd.why.limitOn: The length of all gradients of all numbers together is {len}, more than {limit}. So every gradient is shrunk by the same factor {f}: {g} × {f} = {gu}. This keeps a single unusual batch from throwing the numbers far off.
sd.why.limitOff: All gradients together have length {len}, not more than {limit}, so the gradient stays {g}.
sd.why.mem: Adam does not use the gradient directly. For every number it keeps two running averages: m, the average gradient (its direction, “momentum”), and v, the average squared gradient (how big its gradients usually are). Each step mixes in a little of the new gradient:
sd.why.start: Both averages start at 0, so in the first steps they are too small. Adam corrects this by dividing by 1 − 0.9^{t} = {bc1} and 1 − 0.98^{t} = {bc2} (this is Adam's step {t}; the corrections approach 1 over time).
sd.why.lr: learning rate {lr}: how big the steps are.
sd.why.lrWarm: learning rate {lr}: during the first {w} steps it grows from 0 to {full} (warm-up), so the first steps are small. This is step {t}.
sd.why.ratio: m̂ / √v̂ = {r}. It is near ±1 when the gradients keep pointing the same way, and smaller when they disagree. So every number moves by at most about the learning rate, however big or small its gradient is.
sd.why.matches: ✓ This is exactly the model's number now: {now}.
sd.why.differs: The model's number now is {now} (it has changed since).
jr.title: Follow the tokens through the model
jr.help: This shows one answer as the model computes it, with its real numbers. Every square in a strip is one number; red is positive, blue negative. Reading the animal happens once. Writing repeats: one pass through the model for every token of the answer, and each token it writes goes back in for the next pass.
jr.intro: Press Next to follow the question through the model one stage at a time. “Answer slowly” moves through the stages by itself.
jr.c.tokens: The word “{word}” is cut into letters; in front goes the task token “{task}”, which says what to write. That makes {n} tokens, and every token is a number: its place in the list of tokens the model knows.
jr.c.lookupHead: 2. Every token number picks a row of numbers.
jr.c.lookup: Token “{tok}” is number {id}, so the model takes row {id} of its letter table: {d} numbers. To these it adds the row for the token's position (1st, 2nd, …), so it knows where in the word the token stands. Only these numbers go on; the letters themselves are never used again.
jr.c.read: The {n} rows look at each other (attention: each takes in a little of the others) and think (each row on its own). The result is {d} numbers per input token: the model's reading of the animal. It is kept and used for every letter of the answer.
jr.c.writeFirst: Nothing is written yet, so the task token “{tok}” goes in, at position {pos}. It picks its rows, looks at the animal's numbers, thinks, and its final numbers are compared with every row of the letter table: {v} scores, turned into chances. The highest is “{chosen}” ({p} %).
jr.c.write: The token written last, “{tok}”, goes in at position {pos}. It picks its rows, looks back at the answer so far, looks at the animal's numbers, thinks, and its final numbers are compared with every row of the letter table: {v} scores, turned into chances. The highest is “{chosen}” ({p} %).
jr.c.back: ↩ “{chosen}” is written and goes back in: it is the input of the next pass (position {pos}).
jr.c.end: ■ It wrote “end”: the word is finished. Answer: “{word}”, after {n} passes through the writing part.
jr.lane.write: Writing the answer — one pass per token
jr.s.in: what goes in: letter-table row + position row
jr.s.memory: after reading (what the writer looks at)
jr.s.final: after looking back, looking at the animal, thinking and the volume knobs: these make the guess
jr.modelTip: look back at the answer so far, look at the animal, think, volume knobs
jr.loopTip: This token is the one written in the pass before: it went back in.
jr.d.tokensNote: The model knows {v} tokens: letters of all four languages, the end, task tokens and a few special ones. A chat model cuts text into pieces of words instead and knows about 100,000 tokens, but the idea is the same: text in, numbers in.
jr.d.lookup: The letter table has {v} rows (one per token) of {d} numbers each. The model learned these numbers; at the start they were random. Point at a square to see its value.
jr.d.read: Here every input token looks at every other one. Each row of the table below says how much a token takes in from each of the others (adds up to 100).
jr.d.readAtt: Animal letters looking at each other
jr.d.readOnce: After this the model never reads the letters again. Every pass of the writing part looks at these “after reading” numbers instead.
jr.d.in: “{tok}” = token {id}: its letter-table row + the row for position {pos}.
jr.d.selfTitle: Look back at the answer so far
jr.d.selfFirst: Nothing written yet: it can only look at itself (100 %).
jr.d.self: It looks at the tokens that went in so far (never at later ones: they are not written yet). How much, per head:
jr.d.cross: It looks at the “after reading” numbers of the animal's tokens and takes in a mix of them. How much, per head (also in the reading lane above):
jr.d.think: 64 thinking units switch on or stay off depending on the numbers, and each unit that is on adds its own pattern. Then the volume knobs bring the numbers to a standard size.
jr.d.guess: The final numbers are multiplied with every row of the letter table and added up: {v} scores, one per token. Softmax turns the scores into chances that add up to 100 %. The top 5:
jr.d.pick: It always writes the token with the highest chance: “{chosen}”. (Chat models usually pick by chance, weighted by these percentages, so their answers can differ each time.)
jr.d.inside: See every number of this pass → Inside the model
